title: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition) · Units 83–84
description: B2 vocabulary and noun-pattern practice for uncountable nouns, plural-form equipment, clothing, subject names and agreement.
sourceNotice: Prepared from the user-supplied book for personal study. Vocabulary targets follow source topics and exercise vocabulary; all teaching examples and notes are newly written, and original exercises, extended passages and illustrations are not reproduced.

audit.scope: Teaching text, page illustrations, exercises and relevant answer-key entries reviewed for target vocabulary, noun countability, plural usage, agreement and regional contrasts.
audit.pronunciation: Broad British IPA for common words and shorter expressions. Some regional variants and phonetic detail are not exhaustively represented; actual speech depends on installed browser voices.
audit.languagePolicy: English everywhere except natural Brazilian Portuguese translations under pt.
audit.reviewMethod: Source-pages and answer-key comparison, original example curation, lexical and countability review, and static JSON, ID and audio-target validation. No live app import or browser speech test performed.
audit.limitations: No bundled recordings and no browser TTS, speech recognition or VocabLab round-trip import test. Some plural-form terms also have a singular form in other senses; usage notes distinguish those cases.

units.title: Unit 83 — Uncountable nouns
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 172–173 (PDF pages 173–174).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition)
learningObjectives: Recognise common uncountable nouns and avoid inappropriate articles and plural forms.
Use travel, food, abstract-noun and material vocabulary with correct countability.
Distinguish uncountable nouns from related countable words such as work/job and advice/recommendation.
Apply natural quantities and collocations, including make progress and do research.

items.example: A ticket is a countable noun, so you can buy two tickets.
items.note: A countable noun can take a/an and normally has a plural form.

items.example: Equipment is an uncountable noun in standard English.
items.note: Uncountable nouns normally have no a/an or plural -s in their ordinary mass meaning.

items.example: Could you send me some information about the course?
items.note: Usually uncountable: some information or a piece of information, not an information or informations.

items.example: Her luggage was delivered to the hotel before dinner.
items.note: Uncountable; say an item or piece of luggage to count individual objects.

items.example: Passengers must collect their baggage after landing.
items.note: Uncountable; especially frequent in American English for bags taken on a journey.

items.example: We found affordable accommodation near the conference centre.
items.note: In British English this meaning is normally uncountable; American English also commonly uses accommodations.

items.example: We saved some money for our trip to Scotland.
items.note: Uncountable when referring to money in general; do not use moneys in everyday contexts.

items.example: You can exchange foreign currency at the airport.
items.note: Uncountable for money in general; countable for types, as in several currencies.

items.example: Public transport is reliable in this part of the city.
items.note: Normally uncountable for the service or system; transportation is common in American English.

items.example: International travel has become more expensive.
items.note: Uncountable in the general sense of travelling; use trip or journey for an individual occasion.

items.example: The train journey across the mountains took four hours.
items.note: Countable; often emphasises getting from one place to another.

items.example: They organised a short trip to Edinburgh.
items.note: Countable; refers to an occasion of going somewhere and often returning.

items.example: She is attending a workshop during her business trip.
items.note: Use a business trip for one work-related journey, not a business travel.

items.example: We brought enough food for everyone at the picnic.
items.note: Usually uncountable for food in general; foods can refer to different kinds.

items.example: There is too much sugar in this drink.
items.note: Generally uncountable as an ingredient.

items.example: We served rice with grilled vegetables.
items.note: Uncountable; individual grains can be counted.

items.example: The spaghetti tastes delicious with this sauce.
items.note: Uncountable in English and normally takes a singular verb.

items.example: I spread a little butter on the toast.
items.note: Normally uncountable as a food substance.

items.example: Would you like some fresh bread with the soup?
items.note: Normally uncountable; use a loaf or a slice to identify an amount.

items.example: Add a small amount of flour to thicken the mixture.
items.note: Uncountable as an ingredient.

items.example: There is some vegetable soup in the fridge.
items.note: Usually uncountable; a soup can mean a type or a serving in some contexts.

items.example: My supervisor gave me useful advice before the interview.
items.note: Uncountable; say some advice or a piece of advice, not an advice.

items.example: She has extensive knowledge of computer networks.
items.note: Usually uncountable; the standard form is knowledge, not knowledges.

items.example: Our team has made good progress with the prototype.
items.note: Uncountable; the common collocation is make progress.

items.example: The department is conducting research into battery safety.
items.note: Usually uncountable; use research into/on something rather than researches for projects in general.

items.example: There is still a lot of work to do before the deadline.
items.note: Uncountable for effort or tasks in general; a job is a countable position or task.

items.example: I finished my homework before going to football practice.
items.note: Uncountable; say a homework assignment when counting tasks.

items.example: He has considerable experience of managing projects.
items.note: Uncountable for accumulated knowledge; an experience is a particular event.

items.example: The report examines how wealth is distributed across regions.
items.note: Normally uncountable when referring to being rich or to accumulated assets.

items.example: The charity supports families living in poverty.
items.note: Uncountable in the general sense; avoid a poverty for the condition.

items.example: The trainees made steady progress during the course.
items.note: Use make progress, not make progresses.

items.example: They plan to do research on coastal erosion.
items.note: Research is uncountable in this common verb–noun collocation.

items.example: This cloth is strong enough for outdoor cushions.
items.note: Uncountable for textile material; a cloth can be a particular piece used for cleaning.

items.example: The scarf is made of pure silk.
items.note: Usually uncountable for the textile material.

items.example: The boots are made from soft leather.
items.note: Normally uncountable for the material.

items.example: The walls were built of stone.
items.note: Uncountable for building material; a stone is one individual piece.

items.example: Brick is a common material for traditional houses.
items.note: Can be uncountable for material or countable for individual bricks.

items.example: This container is made of recycled plastic.
items.note: Usually uncountable for material; plastics can describe different types.

items.example: The factory once used coal to generate heat.
items.note: Uncountable as a fuel.

items.example: The country exports oil to neighbouring markets.
items.note: Uncountable for the substance; oils can mean different varieties.

items.example: All the laboratory equipment was inspected this morning.
items.note: Uncountable; use pieces of equipment to count individual devices.

items.example: We installed new software on the test computer.
items.note: Normally uncountable; say a software package or program for one product.

items.example: The news is encouraging for the research team.
items.note: Despite final -s, news is uncountable and takes a singular verb.

items.example: The weather was unusually warm in early October.
items.note: Uncountable; say bad weather, not a bad weather.

items.example: We ordered new furniture for the office.
items.note: Uncountable; count items or pieces of furniture, not furnitures.

items.example: She shared three helpful tips for improving pronunciation.
items.note: Countable counterpart to advice: a tip, several tips.

items.example: The technician was offered a new job in Bristol.
items.note: Countable: a job or jobs; contrasts with uncountable work.

items.example: They published a study of teenagers’ reading habits.
items.note: Countable for a specific investigation; contrasts with uncountable research.

items.example: We added noodles to the vegetable broth.
items.note: Plural count noun; contrasts with uncountable rice in the exercise.

items.example: The organiser has a surprise for the volunteers.
items.note: Countable: a surprise; contrasts with some news.

items.example: The company exports textiles to several countries.
items.note: Plural count noun referring to fabric products; contrasts with cloth as material.

items.example: The panel made three recommendations for improvement.
items.note: Countable; contrasts with uncountable advice.

items.example: A small coin fell out of his pocket.
items.note: Countable; contrasts with money, which is uncountable.

items.example: We bought a loaf of wholemeal bread.
items.note: Countable unit for bread; plural loaves.

items.example: The report contains a surprising fact about the region.
items.note: Countable item of information; information itself is generally uncountable.

items.example: He packed one case for the weekend.
items.note: Countable container for baggage; also means an instance or legal case.

items.pt: pesquisa sobre; investigação a respeito de
items.example: Her research into renewable energy received funding.
items.note: Use research into a topic; research itself is usually uncountable.

items.example: The team began a study of coastal wildlife.
items.note: A study of is a countable expression for one investigation.

items.example: She does voluntary work at an animal shelter.
items.note: Work is uncountable in this expression.

items.example: The museum displays antique furniture from local homes.
items.note: Furniture remains uncountable even with a descriptive adjective.

items.example: They booked a package holiday that includes airport transfers.
items.note: Countable trip package; transport and accommodation in it are often uncountable.

items.example: Drizzle a little olive oil over the vegetables.
items.note: Uncountable food substance listed as a suitable extension in the exercises.

items.example: Add salt only after tasting the soup.
items.note: Uncountable as a cooking ingredient.

items.example: There is some milk in the fridge.
items.note: Normally uncountable in ordinary food contexts.

items.example: She sweetens her tea with honey.
items.note: Usually uncountable as food.

items.example: The jumper is knitted from natural wool.
items.note: Uncountable for the fibre or textile.

items.example: This shirt is made from organic cotton.
items.note: Uncountable for material.

items.example: The seals are made of flexible rubber.
items.note: Uncountable for material; a rubber in British English can also mean an eraser.

items.example: The workers mixed cement for the repairs.
items.note: Uncountable building material.

items.example: The frame is made of lightweight metal.
items.note: Usually uncountable for material; metals can mean different kinds.

items.example: The shelves are made of solid wood.
items.note: Uncountable for the material; a wood can mean a small forest.

items.example: The contractor ordered timber for the roof.
items.note: Uncountable for wood prepared for building.

items.example: The door is made of reinforced glass.
items.note: Uncountable for the material; a glass is a drinking vessel.

items.example: The factory uses gas to heat the building.
items.note: Normally uncountable as a fuel; gases refers to different gases.

items.example: The building produces some of its own electricity.
items.note: Uncountable resource.

items.example: Steam escaped from the old machine.
items.note: Usually uncountable for water vapour.

items.example: The research station runs partly on solar power.
items.note: Uncountable form of energy.

items.example: We stopped to buy petrol before leaving town.
items.note: Uncountable; American English generally uses gasoline or gas in this sense.

sectionsChecked: D: Abstract uncountable nouns and nouns for activities

units.title: Unit 84 — Words that only occur in the plural
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 174–175 (PDF pages 175–176).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition)
learningObjectives: Recognise tools, clothing and equipment normally named with plural-form nouns.
Use the correct agreement and counting constructions for plural-form nouns.
Distinguish plural-form words for contents, places, money and sound from singular senses.
Treat subjects and game names such as physics and billiards as singular where appropriate, while identifying genuine plural subject labels.

items.example: These scissors are sharp enough to cut thick paper.
items.note: Plural in form and takes a plural verb; say a pair of scissors for one instrument.

items.example: The electrician used pliers to grip the wire.
items.note: Plural-form tool; use a pair of pliers when counting instruments.

items.example: My earphones are small enough to fit in my pocket.
items.note: Plural in form; refers to small listening devices worn in or near the ears.

items.example: I used tweezers to remove the tiny splinter.
items.note: Plural-form tool; count a pair of tweezers.

items.example: Use tongs to turn the vegetables on the grill.
items.note: Plural-form gripping tool; often a pair of tongs.

items.example: These headphones block much of the background noise.
items.note: Normally plural for a set worn over or on the ears.

items.example: The visitors used binoculars to watch the birds.
items.note: Plural-form optical instrument; say a pair of binoculars.

items.example: The kitchen scales are on the counter.
items.note: Plural-form weighing device in British English; a set of scales weighs objects.

items.example: The officer carried handcuffs on her belt.
items.note: Plural-form restraining device; a pair of handcuffs.

items.example: The gardener used shears to trim the hedge.
items.note: Plural-form cutting tool, often larger than scissors.

items.example: His glasses were on the desk beside the monitor.
items.note: Plural for spectacles; contrast with a glass for drinking.

items.example: She put on her spectacles to read the small print.
items.note: Plural-form alternative to glasses, often rather formal or old-fashioned.

items.pt: óculos de proteção; óculos de natação
items.example: Everyone must wear safety goggles in the workshop.
items.note: Plural-form eyewear protecting the eyes from water, dust or chemicals.

items.example: Her clothes were still drying on the line.
items.note: Plural noun without an ordinary singular meaning one garment; use an item of clothing.

items.example: My pyjamas are made of soft cotton.
items.note: Plural-form clothing word; British spelling pyjamas, US pajamas.

items.example: She bought some new knickers at the shop.
items.note: British English for women’s underwear; plural-form word.

items.example: He packed an extra pair of pants for the trip.
items.note: In British English this can mean underpants; in American English pants usually means trousers.

items.example: These underpants are made from breathable fabric.
items.note: Plural-form term for underwear worn below the waist.

items.example: My jeans are too long, so I need to shorten them.
items.note: Plural-form garment; say a pair of jeans for one item.

items.example: She wore thick tights under her skirt.
items.note: British English for close-fitting legwear; usually plural.

items.example: The mechanics wear overalls to protect their clothes.
items.note: Plural-form work garment; usage varies regionally for types of protective clothing.

items.example: Her leggings are comfortable for stretching exercises.
items.note: Plural-form close-fitting trousers.

items.example: The painter wore blue dungarees over a T-shirt.
items.note: British English term for bib overalls; plural form.

items.example: These shorts are perfect for hot weather.
items.note: Plural-form clothing word; one pair of shorts.

items.example: His trousers were covered in mud.
items.note: Plural-form garment in British English; American English uses pants.

items.example: He wore braces to keep his trousers in place.
items.note: British English; American English calls these suspenders.

items.example: He bought new swimming trunks for the pool.
items.note: Plural-form garment worn by men for swimming.

items.example: The graphics in this video game look realistic.
items.note: Pictures produced by a computer; plural verb in this meaning.

items.example: The goods were delivered yesterday afternoon.
items.note: Plural-form word for items for sale or transport; the goods are, not is.

items.example: The engineers checked the foundations of the new bridge.
items.note: Plural when referring to structural supports; singular foundation exists in other uses.

items.example: Smoking is prohibited on these premises.
items.note: Plural-form noun for a building or land occupied by an organisation.

items.example: The local authorities have approved the event.
items.note: Usually plural when referring to officials or governing bodies; authority also exists as a singular noun.

items.example: The organisation moved its headquarters to Manchester.
items.note: Plural in form; one headquarters may take singular or plural agreement depending on usage.

items.example: The acoustics in the auditorium are excellent.
items.note: Plural when describing sound quality; acoustics as a scientific subject can take a singular verb.

items.example: The contents of the parcel were damaged in transit.
items.note: Plural for things inside a container; distinguish from uncountable content for subject matter.

items.example: His looks are less important to her than his kindness.
items.note: Plural noun for physical appearance; a look can mean a glance or style.

items.example: They rented a small house on the outskirts of town.
items.note: Plural-form noun; say on the outskirts of a place.

items.example: Turn right at the traffic lights near the station.
items.note: Often plural for a set of signals at a junction; a traffic light can refer to one signal.

items.example: The stairs are slippery after cleaning.
items.note: Usually plural for a staircase; a stair can mean a single step.

items.pt: arrecadação; receita obtida com uma venda ou evento
items.example: The proceeds from the raffle will support the library.
items.note: Plural noun for money obtained from an activity or sale; proceeds go to a cause.

items.example: The missing hiker’s whereabouts are still unknown.
items.note: Plural-form noun referring to where someone or something is.

items.example: Billiards is popular at the club on Friday evenings.
items.note: Game name ending in -s; normally singular verb when referring to the game.

items.example: Dominoes is a relaxing game for a rainy afternoon.
items.note: The game name may take a singular verb; dominoes are individual playing pieces.

items.example: Draughts is played on a chequered board.
items.note: British name for the game called checkers in American English.

items.example: Darts is a popular game in many British pubs.
items.note: Usually singular agreement for the sport; individual darts are countable.

items.example: Bowls is often played outdoors on a green.
items.note: The game name takes singular agreement; individual bowls are countable objects.

items.example: Cards is a favourite pastime in their family.
items.note: Can refer collectively to a game with playing cards; cards as individual objects is plural.

items.example: Physics is her strongest subject at university.
items.note: School subject with final -s but normally a singular verb.

items.example: Economics is taught in the first year of the programme.
items.note: As an academic subject, usually a singular verb.

items.example: Classics is offered as an optional degree course.
items.note: Academic study of ancient Greek and Roman languages and cultures; subject name often takes a singular verb.

items.example: Gymnastics is an Olympic sport.
items.note: Activity name with -s, generally treated as singular.

items.example: Athletics is widely followed during the summer games.
items.note: Sport name; usually singular agreement when treated as a discipline.

items.example: The latest news is available on the website.
items.note: Not plural grammatically despite ending in -s; news takes a singular verb.

items.example: The spaghetti was ready before the sauce.
items.note: An Italian plural form, but treated as uncountable and singular in English.

items.example: This television series is set in northern England.
items.note: Same form in singular and plural: one series is, two series are.

items.example: A bicycle is an economical means of transport.
items.note: Same form in singular and plural: a means is, several means are.

items.example: Both socks have small holes near the heel.
items.note: Ordinary plural of sock; unlike trousers, a single sock is valid.

items.example: This shirt needs ironing before tomorrow.
items.note: Ordinary singular count noun, unlike plural-only clothing words.

items.example: Ethics is part of the nursing curriculum.
items.note: Singular agreement for the subject; someone’s ethics may take plural agreement for moral principles.

items.example: Politics is an interesting field of study.
items.note: Often singular for the subject; plural agreement occurs when referring to someone’s political views.

items.example: Genetics is central to modern medical research.
items.note: Academic subject name ending in -s and taking singular agreement.

items.example: The arts are an important part of the city’s cultural life.
items.note: Plural word for creative disciplines; also used in arts subjects and courses.

items.example: The humanities are represented in the new research centre.
items.note: A plural subject-area label; normally uses a plural verb.

items.example: The natural sciences are essential to this course.
items.note: Plural subject-area label; do not automatically give it singular agreement.

items.example: I keep a pair of scissors in the first drawer.
items.note: A pair of provides a countable unit for a plural-form instrument.

items.example: He ordered a pair of trousers online.
items.note: One garment is a pair of trousers, not a trouser.

items.example: Visitors must wear badges while on the premises.
items.note: Fixed expression meaning inside or within the relevant building or grounds.

D: Words with plural form but used mostly with singular verbs
